A working lesson · Civil procedure · Federal courts

The Erie Doctrine

In 1934, Harry Tompkins lost his right arm to a passing freight train in Pennsylvania and sued the railroad. Whether he won turned less on the accident than on which courthouse his lawyer picked. This lesson teaches the doctrine that grew out of that problem: which law a federal court applies in a diversity case, and the method for deciding it.

Federal court, S.D.N.Y.

Under the "general law" federal judges then applied, Tompkins counts roughly as a licensee. The railroad owes him ordinary care. He can win — and did: a jury gave him $30,000.

Pennsylvania state court

Under Pennsylvania case law, a man walking beside the tracks is a trespasser. The railroad is liable only for wanton or willful conduct. He almost certainly loses.

Before anything else — commitungraded

Today, a diversity case like Tompkins's raises questions of both kinds. Two of them:

Q1. What duty did the railroad owe a man walking beside its tracks?
Q2. How many days does the railroad get to file its answer to the complaint?

Whose answers does the federal judge use — Pennsylvania's, or the federal courts' own?

The path: §1 how the problem arose and how Erie answered it · §2 the test for questions no federal directive answers · §3 what happens when a Federal Rule is on point · §4 the modern hard case · §5 the assembled method · then a closed-book final where you rule on nine motions.

Next · §1 From Swift to Erie ↓

§1 · History

From Swift to Erie

The doctrine begins with one statute and a reading of it that lasted ninety-six years. Every case in this lesson is a response to what that reading caused.

28 U.S.C. § 1652  The Rules of Decision Act
LII ↗ On the books since 1789. Every fight in this lesson is about what its words cover.
The text, verbatim
"The laws of the several states, except where the Constitution or treaties of the United States or Acts of Congress otherwise require or provide, shall be regarded as rules of decision in civil actions in the courts of the United States, in cases where they apply."28 U.S.C. § 1652 — complete text of the section
What turned on one word

In Swift v. Tyson (1842), Justice Story read "the laws of the several states" to mean state statutes and local usages — not state court decisions. On questions of "general" law, like commercial contracts, federal judges could decide for themselves what the law was. Story hoped state courts would adopt this federal "general law" and commercial law would become uniform nationwide. State courts did not go along.

The result

Two bodies of common law grew side by side. On the same facts, a state court applied its own precedents while the federal courthouse across the street applied "general law." Any party who could get into federal court could pick whichever rule favored it.

Predict the exploit — commitungraded

It is 1926. You run Brown & Yellow Taxicab, a Kentucky company. You want an exclusive pickup contract with a railroad — a monopoly deal that Kentucky's courts refuse to enforce, but federal "general law" would enforce. Your competitor, Black & White Taxicab, is also a Kentucky company, so there is no diversity of citizenship and no way into federal court. What do you do?

The chain, Swift to Erie
1
Swift v. Tyson (1842). "Laws" means statutes, not decisions. Federal courts apply their own "general law."
2
The incentive. Same claim, two answers — the outcome depends on which courthouse hears it.
3
The exploit. Brown & Yellow reincorporates in Tennessee to manufacture diversity, then wins under general law (Black & White Taxicab, 1928).
4
The embarrassment. Forum shopping is now a strategy, and the promised uniformity never arrived.
5
Erie R.R. v. Tompkins (1938). Swift overruled. State law — decisions included — governs substantive questions.
6
The new problem. Which questions count as "substantive"? That fight fills the rest of the lesson.

Watch the chain, or read it on the left: each step is somebody responding to the incentive the previous step created. The taxicab case is the one you just predicted — a company dissolved itself and reincorporated in another state for the sole purpose of suing its Kentucky rival in a federal courtroom, where the contract Kentucky would not enforce was enforceable. The Supreme Court let the judgment stand. Holmes dissented, and ten years later the Court adopted his view.

Note what the exploit shows: under Swift, the "accident" of corporate citizenship changed who owned a legal right. That is the specific unfairness Erie set out to end, and the reason the doctrine exists at all.

304 U.S. 64 (1938)  Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins
LII ↗ Swift overruled. In diversity, state law governs substantive questions — whoever declared it.
The holding, verbatim
"Except in matters governed by the Federal Constitution or by acts of Congress, the law to be applied in any case is the law of the state. And whether the law of the state shall be declared by its Legislature in a statute or by its highest court in a decision is not a matter of federal concern. There is no federal general common law."Erie R.R. v. Tompkins, 304 U.S. 64, 78 (1938) — one continuous passage
Why the Court overruled Swift

Brandeis gave three reasons. First, new historical research showed Swift had misread the Act — "the laws" was meant to include court decisions. Second, the regime discriminated: only a party who could invoke diversity got to choose the better law, so out-of-state parties held rights their in-state opponents did not. Third, the Constitution grants no power, to Congress or the courts, to declare substantive common law for the states — which is why the opinion says there is no federal general common law.

What Erie did for Tompkins
The Second Circuit had affirmed his $30,000 verdict under general law. The Supreme Court reversed and sent the case back to be decided under Pennsylvania law — the trespasser rule included. The accident of the parties' citizenship no longer changed the substantive rule.

§2 · The state-law track

Substance, procedure, and the twin aims

Erie says state law governs "substantive" questions. It does not say which questions those are. Three cases — York, Byrd, and Hanna — built the test federal courts still use when no federal directive answers the question.

Scenario — commitungraded

1945. A beneficiary sues a trustee in federal court under diversity, asking for equitable relief. New York's limitation period on the claim has run. Federal courts sitting in equity traditionally used their own flexible timeliness doctrine instead of a fixed clock. May the federal court hear the case?

326 U.S. 99 (1945)  Guaranty Trust Co. v. York
LII ↗ Forget the labels — ask whether the choice of rule changes the result.
The test, verbatim
"…the outcome of the litigation in the federal court should be substantially the same, so far as legal rules determine the outcome of a litigation, as it would be if tried in a State court."Guaranty Trust Co. v. York, 326 U.S. 99, 109 (1945)
The reasoning

Frankfurter refused to fight about the words "substance" and "procedure" — a limitation period is "procedural" for some purposes and "substantive" for others. Erie's point was that moving a case across the street should not change who wins. So the test became: would applying the federal practice instead of the state rule significantly affect the result? If yes, the state rule governs. The expired New York clock barred the claim in state court, so it barred the claim in federal court too.

Push on the test — commitungraded

Take York's test literally: does the choice of rule change the outcome? Now apply it to a rule about how court papers are served. Serve them the wrong way and the case can be dismissed. Is the service rule outcome-determinative?

Three cases, one test taking shape
1
York (1945). Outcome decides: if the state rule would change the result, apply it.
2
The overshoot. After the fact, almost any rule can change a result. Read literally, York federalizes nothing and state-ifies everything.
3
Byrd (1958). Outcome is not the only interest. Where the state rule is not bound up with the underlying right, strong federal interests — here, the jury's role — go on the scale.
4
Hanna (1965), in dictum. Judge the difference ex ante — at forum-choice time — against the twin aims: forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws.
356 U.S. 525 (1958)  Byrd v. Blue Ridge
LII ↗

An injured lineman's status as a "statutory employee" decided whether he could sue at all. South Carolina practice gave that question to the judge; federal practice gives it to the jury. The Court held the state practice was not bound up with the rights the state statute created — it was just how South Carolina divided work between judge and jury — and the federal system's interest in the jury's province, reinforced by the Seventh Amendment's influence, outweighed a speculative effect on outcome. The federal jury practice governed. The lesson: outcome-determination is not mechanical; federal interests can push back.

Byrd narrowed York from one side. Hanna finished the job from the other, and its version is the one you apply on an exam — the next card.

380 U.S. 460 (1965)  Hanna v. Plumer — the twin aims
LII ↗ Judge the state-federal difference at the moment the plaintiff chooses a forum.
The aims, verbatim
…the twin aims of the Erie rule: "discouragement of forum-shopping and avoidance of inequitable administration of the laws."Hanna v. Plumer, 380 U.S. 460, 468 (1965)
How to run the test

Stand at the courthouse door, before filing, and ask two questions about the state-federal difference. Would it pull a rational plaintiff into federal court to get a better substantive result? And would tolerating it mean out-of-state parties get a materially better version of the law than the locals stuck in state court? If either answer is yes, apply the state rule. If the difference is one nobody would choose a forum over — trivial housekeeping — the federal court may follow its own practice. This is York's test moved to the moment of forum choice: measure the difference ex ante, not after the case has collapsed on a technicality.

Worked example
A state's two-year limitation period against the federal courts' older, more forgiving equity practice: a plaintiff with a stale claim would file federal every time, and locals would be barred while diverse plaintiffs proceeded. Both aims fire — state law governs. That is York's result, reproduced by Hanna's method.

§3 · The Federal-Rule track

When a Federal Rule is on point: Hanna and Walker

Everything in §2 assumed no federal directive answered the question. Hanna's actual holding covers the other case: when a Federal Rule of Civil Procedure speaks to the disputed question, the Erie cases drop out entirely, and a different statute takes over.

Scenario — commitungraded

Diversity suit in Massachusetts federal court against an estate's executor. The process server leaves the summons and complaint at the executor's home with his wife — exactly what Federal Rule 4 then allowed. Massachusetts law required in-hand delivery to an executor. Service ends the case if it was defective — surely outcome-determinative. Valid service?

28 U.S.C. § 2072  The Rules Enabling Act
LII ↗ Congress's delegation: the Supreme Court writes the Federal Rules, within one limit.
The text, verbatim
(a) "The Supreme Court shall have the power to prescribe general rules of practice and procedure and rules of evidence for cases in the United States district courts (including proceedings before magistrate judges thereof) and courts of appeals."

(b) "Such rules shall not abridge, enlarge or modify any substantive right. All laws in conflict with such rules shall be of no further force or effect after such rules have taken effect."28 U.S.C. § 2072(a)–(b)
Subsection (c), quoted in full

(c) "Such rules may define when a ruling of a district court is final for the purposes of appeal under section 1291 of this title."

Why this changes the track

Look back at the Rules of Decision Act in §1: state laws govern "except where … Acts of Congress otherwise require or provide." The Enabling Act is an Act of Congress, and a Federal Rule made under it carries that authority. So when a valid Rule answers the disputed question, the RDA's own text steps aside — no outcome test, no twin aims. The only question left is validity under § 2072(b).

380 U.S. 460 (1965)  Hanna v. Plumer — the holding
LII ↗ Rule 4 answered the service question, so Rule 4 governed. Massachusetts law never entered the analysis.
The validity test, verbatim
"The test must be whether a rule really regulates procedure, — the judicial process for enforcing rights and duties recognized by substantive law and for justly administering remedy and redress for disregard or infraction of them." … "The Erie rule has never been invoked to void a Federal Rule."Hanna, 380 U.S. at 464 (quoting Sibbach v. Wilson & Co., 312 U.S. 1, 14 (1941)); id. at 470
What Hanna holds

Service under Rule 4 was valid. When a Federal Rule covers the disputed question, its validity is measured against the Enabling Act and the Constitution — not against York's outcome test, and not against the twin aims. A Rule that really regulates procedure may apply even though it changes how this case comes out. And the presumption of validity is powerful in practice: the Court has never struck down a Federal Rule under § 2072(b).

446 U.S. 740 (1980)  Walker v. Armco Steel Corp.
LII ↗ "On point" is a real question. Read the Rule for what it actually answers.
The facts

Oklahoma tort suit in federal court. Under Oklahoma law, an action "commences" for limitations purposes only when the defendant is served. Walker filed his complaint inside the two-year window but served Armco after it closed. Rule 3 says:

Rule 3, verbatim
"A civil action is commenced by filing a complaint with the court."Fed. R. Civ. P. 3 — complete text of the rule
The holding, verbatim
"Application of the Hanna analysis is premised on a 'direct collision' between the Federal Rule and the state law." … "There is no indication that the Rule was intended to toll a state statute of limitations, much less that it purported to displace state tolling rules for purposes of state statutes of limitations."Walker v. Armco Steel Corp., 446 U.S. 740, 749–51 (1980)
Why Walker is not Hanna

The disputed question was not "when do federal deadlines start running" — Rule 3 answers that. It was "did filing stop Oklahoma's limitations clock" — and Rule 3 says nothing about state tolling. No Rule on point means no Hanna track. The analysis returns to §2, where a limitations rule is exactly what the twin aims protect: state law governed, and Walker's claim was barred.

Hanna — Rule on point

Disputed question: was service valid?

Rule 4 states how service may be made. The Rule answers the very question in dispute.

Result: Enabling Act track. Rule valid → Rule governs. State in-hand requirement displaced.

Walker — no Rule on point

Disputed question: did filing stop the state clock?

Rule 3 sets the start of federal procedural deadlines. It does not mention state limitations or tolling.

Result: No direct collision → back to the state-law track. Twin aims fire → Oklahoma rule governs.

§4 · The hard case

Shady Grove

The modern test case. Everything from §2 and §3 collides in one suit — and the Court split three ways on how the method should run.

Scenario — commitungraded

Allstate owes Shady Grove, a medical clinic, about $500 of statutory interest on a late insurance payment. New York's § 901(b) says a suit for a statutory penalty may not proceed as a class action. Federal Rule 23 says a class action "may be maintained" if its listed requirements are met. Shady Grove files a class action in federal court for every New Yorker Allstate paid late — over $5 million. First question on the method: does Rule 23 answer the disputed question, "may this suit proceed as a class action"?

559 U.S. 393 (2010)  Shady Grove Orthopedic Associates v. Allstate
LII ↗ Five votes that Rule 23 controls — but no majority on the validity test.
The collision

Five justices held that Rule 23 and § 901(b) answer the same question — may this suit be maintained as a class action? — and give opposite answers. That is a direct collision, so the case moved to validity under § 2072(b). (Ginsburg, dissenting for four, would have read Rule 23 narrowly to avoid the collision, treating § 901(b) as a limit on the remedy rather than on class procedure.)

Two validity tests, verbatim anchors
Scalia, plurality (4)

Test the Rule on its face, not its effects in this case: is it a rule that "really regulates procedure"? Rule 23 plainly is. Valid, full stop.

Stevens, concurring (the 5th vote)

A Rule cannot displace a state law "so intertwined with a state right or remedy that it functions to define the scope of the state-created right." § 901(b) is a freestanding procedural limit, not part of any right's definition — so Rule 23 validly applies here.

Quoted phrases: Scalia's from Sibbach as quoted in the plurality opinion; Stevens's from his concurrence. Which test controls remains unsettled — many lower courts follow Stevens as the narrowest ground. Know both for an exam.

The result
The class action proceeded in federal court — a suit New York's own courts would have refused to certify, with exposure three orders of magnitude beyond the individual claim. Shady Grove shows the Hanna track's consequence: a valid Rule applies even when it visibly invites forum shopping.

§5 · The method

The full method

Every case you have met is one node of a single decision path. Watch it assemble and trace three cases through it — then rebuild it yourself from memory.

The decision path — with three cases traced
Chart hidden during the rebuild — finish the exercise below to bring it back.
Step 0. Name the disputed question precisely. Not "service" — "was leaving the summons with his wife valid service?"
NO → state-law track (below)
Step 1. Does a federal directive — Constitution, federal statute, or Federal Rule — answer that question? (Walker: it must be a direct collision, not a shared subject.)
YES → test its validity
Invalid → state-law track
(has never happened to a Rule)
Step 2 — Rule track. Valid under § 2072? It must really regulate procedure and "not abridge, enlarge or modify any substantive right." (Shady Grove: facial test per the plurality; Stevens asks if the state law is intertwined with the right.)
Valid → apply the federal directive
(Hanna, Shady Grove)
Either aim fires → apply state law
(Erie, York, Walker)
Step 3 — state-law track. No directive on point. Twin aims, ex ante: would using federal practice encourage forum shopping, or work inequitable administration of the laws?
Neither fires → federal practice may be followed
Byrd check, on the state-law track: if the state rule is not bound up with the right and a strong federal interest (like the jury's role) pushes back, weigh it.

Final: nine rulings

You are the district judge. Nine motions, each turning on one choice-of-law ruling, decided without the reference shelf — it unlocks again the moment every motion is decided.

Standing facts for all nine motions Every case below is a diversity action in a United States district court. The substantive claims arise under state law. Rule on each motion as the current doctrine requires.

Progress

Mastery checklist

○History. Tell the Swift-to-Erie story as a causal chain and state Erie's holding and its three reasons.
○The state-law track. Run the twin aims ex ante on a fresh difference, and say when Byrd's balance enters.
○The Federal-Rule track. Decide whether a Rule is genuinely on point, state the § 2072(b) test, and explain why Hanna and Walker differ.
○Shady Grove. Find the collision and state both validity tests.
○The method. Rebuild the decision path from memory and run it on new facts, in writing.
○The final. All nine motions ruled on, closed book.
All gates clear. Finish with the transfer task below.

Transfer task

This week, take one Erie hypo from your casebook, class notes, or an old exam your professor released, and write the method paragraph for it: name the disputed question, sort the track, run the right test, and end with a sentence that starts "State law governs because…" or "The Rule applies because…". Bring it to office hours if any step felt uncertain — the sort in step 1 is where most exam answers go wrong.

What this lesson does not teach

  • Your course controls. This lesson uses the canonical cases and the standard modern sequence. If your professor frames the test differently — some teach Byrd as a dead letter, some make it central — the exam answer is your professor's version.
  • Out of scope: Gasperini (damage-cap review standards), Semtek (claim preclusion), Stewart v. Ricoh and § 1404(a) (federal statutes on point), Klaxon and choice of law (which state's law), certification to state courts, and the surviving enclaves of specialized federal common law. Erie eliminated general federal common law only.
  • Simplifications to know about: whether Stevens's Shady Grove concurrence controls under the narrowest-grounds rule is disputed; Byrd's current force is debated; Walker reserved whether Rule 3 tolls limitations for federal-question claims (it can — West v. Conrail).
  • This is a study aid, not legal advice, and no substitute for reading the assigned cases in full.

Quick Reference
RDA § 1652
State laws are the rules of decision in federal civil actions — except where the Constitution or Acts of Congress provide otherwise. Post-Erie, "laws" includes state court decisions.
REA § 2072
The Supreme Court prescribes the Federal Rules (a); they "shall not abridge, enlarge or modify any substantive right" (b). A valid Rule counts as an Act-of-Congress directive under the RDA's exception clause.
Swift (1842)
"Laws" = statutes only; federal courts applied their own "general law." Produced two rule-sets and forum shopping.
Erie (1938)
Swift overruled. In diversity, state law — decisions included — governs substantive questions. "There is no federal general common law." Reasons: Swift misread the Act; discrimination against in-state parties; no constitutional power.
York (1945)
Outcome-determination: federal result should be substantially the same as the state result. Applied the state limitations period in equity.
Byrd (1958)
On the state-law track: if the state rule is not bound up with the right, strong federal interests (judge/jury allocation) can outweigh a speculative outcome effect.
Hanna (1965) — twin aims
No directive on point: judge the difference ex ante against forum shopping and inequitable administration. Trivial differences → federal practice fine.
Hanna (1965) — holding
A Federal Rule on point is tested only under the REA and Constitution ("really regulates procedure"). No Rule has ever been voided.
Walker (1980)
Hanna needs a direct collision. Rule 3 ("commenced by filing") does not toll state limitations — so no collision, state rule governed.
Shady Grove (2010)
Rule 23 collides with NY § 901(b); class action proceeds. Validity split — Scalia (4): facial "really regulates procedure." Stevens (5th vote): invalid as applied only if the state law is intertwined with the state right. Courts split on which controls.
The method
0 Name the disputed question · 1 Federal directive answering it? · 2 Yes → validity (§ 2072) → apply it · 3 No → twin aims ex ante (+ Byrd weighing) → state law if either aim fires.
